extracted.intended_audience: mathematics journal editors, referees, mathematicians, and researchers interested in peer review practices
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and evaluative criteria for checking the correctness of mathematical papers during journal peer review, including expectations of referees, editors' practices, and community validation over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two central judgements in peer review: significance and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review in mathematics involves two key judgements: first, the importance or significance of the results; second, the soundness of the methods employed or, in mathematics, the correctness of the proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often split these two steps (quick opinions on importance followed by technical refereeing for correctness). Significance is judged more subjectively; correctness is treated as more objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary responsibility for correctness lies with the author
rubrics_metrics.description: All interviewees agreed that the primary responsibility for correctness falls on the author: 'In the end it’s the author’s responsibility to make it correct. If there’s a mistake, it’s not the referee’s fault.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not treat peer review as an 'error-catching service' and must vouch for their results. Official guidelines (AMS, EMS) echo this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee must be 'reasonably convinced' of the accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Official guidance and editors' expectations: 'the referee must be reasonably convinced of the accuracy of the paper' and should 'convince themselves it’s most likely to be true'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice this often means a plausibility check combined with checking key steps; referees may state varying degrees of confidence in reports (e.g., 'I can certify everything is correct' vs 'I did not check everything in detail').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal vs practical depth of checking (check every line vs plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally referees would check every line; in practice referees often do plausibility checks, verify techniques they recognize, and focus on likely problematic parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors accept a range of thoroughness; for important papers more exhaustive checking is expected. Referees should indicate in reports how much they checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted checking of 'key places' and suspicious steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees typically do not read line-by-line but identify 'key places' or parts that look 'suspicious' and focus detailed checking there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expertise to find where gaps or non-routine steps may hide errors; check surprising or novel claims in more depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable omission of routine steps (intentional gaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing proofs, authors commonly omit routine steps; such omissions are an accepted part of communication so long as they rely on shared practices of proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should distinguish between acceptable 'routine' omissions and gaps that hide substantial errors; what counts as routine can vary and requires judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling gaps: request clarifications or accept revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When referees encounter 'gaps' they may ask authors to fill them; often authors can rewrite or fill gaps, but sometimes gaps remain unsolvable and the paper may be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/referees should request clarifying revisions and judge whether the author's response satisfactorily fills the gap; persistent unresolved gaps can justify rejection or withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish technical refereeing from 'quick opinions' (division of labour)
rubrics_metrics.description: At many journals editors solicit 'quick opinions' on significance from senior mathematicians and then ask technical referees (often more junior) to check correctness in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign tasks according to willingness and available time; use senior figures for importance assessment and competent, detail-oriented referees for technical checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting referees with the necessary expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must find referees who have the specific expertise needed to understand and check details; in some cases only a handful of people can perform full verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When methods span subfields, solicit referees from each subfield; be aware that obscure specialization may limit referee options and slow review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of reports proportional to paper importance and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Most mathematical papers receive one report because detailed refereeing is time-consuming; top or especially noteworthy papers may receive two or more reports, and multi-disciplinary methods may require multiple referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should weigh the labor cost against the paper's significance; request additional reports when stakes are high or when the first report is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and effort expectations for refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing mathematics is time-consuming—editors reported averages of roughly 8–10 hours, often much more (e.g., 50 hours or weeks of concentrated work) depending on difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should set realistic timelines and be prepared for long review durations; consider allocating complex papers to referees with available time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of author reputation when allocating scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Because refereeing is single-blind, referees often take authors' reputations into account and may read the proofs more or less carefully depending on the author’s track record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can be an efficiency tactic (trust established authors more) but introduces bias; double-blind review has been proposed to counter such bias though may be impractical in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity policy and bias (single-blind vs double-blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is typically single-blind; double-blind has been contentious because referees can often infer authorship and preprints reveal authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should balance inclusivity/bias concerns against practicalities; AMS introduced double-anonymous review in select journals to mitigate implicit bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of close/referee-author relationships for technical checks
rubrics_metrics.description: For technical correctness, having referees who are close to the author or suggested by the author can sometimes be acceptable because correctness is considered (near) objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should still manage conflicts of interest but may permit trusted colleagues to perform technical verification when appropriate and transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting transparency about how much was checked
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee reports vary in granularity—from certainties to admissions of partial checking ('I did not check everything in detail')—and this affects editors' confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should explicitly state the extent of their checking; editors can request further detail or a second report if a report is too sketchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanity checks against known results (plausibility checking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees often compare results to what they know to see whether outcomes are reasonable; surprising results attract more detailed scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use domain knowledge to perform plausibility checks before investing time in full verification; flag surprising claims for deeper checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on community knowledge and post-publication scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication is often only the first step; the mathematical community's subsequent use and scrutiny over time provide further validation. Important results are expected to 'stand the test of time'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and prize committees may require a waiting period (e.g., two years) and general community acceptance before awarding prizes or full trust in a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal verification vs traditional proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some argue for formal (computer-verifiable) proofs to avoid mistakes, but formal proofs are 'unreadable' and not standard practice; most journals handle traditional human-readable proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the trade-off: formal proofs provide full machine-checkable correctness but are currently impractical as routine practice; consider formal methods for especially delicate/critical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability of referees and journal prestige effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are held to higher standards at elite journals; referees invited by top journals tend to perform more thorough checks and know their reports will be judged by leading experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors of top journals should expect and demand more detailed technical reports; referees should be aware of reputational accountability when accepting invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' decision thresholds when reports are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sometimes receive 'too sketchy' reports and must decide whether to request another report or to accept/suboptimally publish a paper due to delays and scarce referee labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should balance the cost of further delay against the risk of publishing unchecked errors; consider soliciting additional or more junior referees when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with community disagreement over proof status
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be genuine disagreements about whether a written argument constitutes a proof (e.g., Mochizuki's abc papers); refereeing may not resolve such disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should note community contention, possibly solicit further reports, and acknowledge that publication may not equate to immediate community acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic replication: refereeing as reproducing the reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing in mathematics can be seen as 'diagnostic replication'—evaluating the truth of a claim by reproducing the reasoning in the paper rather than reproducing external experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach refereeing as reconstruction/verification of the discovered proof; this can require significant cognitive work distinct from empirical replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints: scarcity of referee labor shapes procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Because technical refereeing is burdensome, journals typically limit duplication of refereeing effort (often only one report) and deploy scarce reviewer labor strategically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should design workflows (quick opinions, targeted technical checks) to deploy scarce referee effort efficiently while guarding correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community acceptance as necessary but not sufficient for prizes and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Some prizes require not only publication but also a period of community acceptance after publication (e.g., Clay Millennium rules require at least two years and general acceptance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that publication is a step toward validation; award processes may require additional time and consensus.
